component.name: Tuni
component.summary: Terminals, projects, files, and Git in one window

description.p: Tuni is a terminal workspace. A window holds projects, a project holds tabs, and a tab holds a niri-style layout of panes — each one a terminal, a file, or a diff.

The terminal is Ghostty's own emulation, through libghostty-vt: the VT parser, the grid, reflow, scrollback, Kitty keyboard encoding, SGR mouse reporting, and 574 color themes that paint the window as well as the terminal.
Around it:

ul.li: A file tree of the directory the focused shell is working in
A Git panel that stages, commits, and pushes by running git itself
An editor with syntax highlighting, and a diff viewer that stages a hunk at a time
A command palette, a find bar over the terminal, and a most-recently-used tab switcher
A session that comes back the way it was left

description.p: The install command works in fish. It was written as bash <(curl ...), which is process substitution and something fish does not have, so the shell answered "Invalid redirection target" instead of installing anything. It is a pipe into bash now, which every shell understands and which costs nothing here: the installer's menu reads its keys from the terminal rather than from standard input.
The build instructions name every package a build needs rather than four of them, and name separately the ones that only the checks want.

Tuni checks whether a newer Tuni has been released. No package repository carries it yet, so nothing on the machine would otherwise notice one; the window asks the release page once per run and offers an Update button that opens the installer in a tab of its own, where sudo has somewhere to ask for a password. The check turns off under Preferences, Terminal, Updates.

That installer is a script anyone can run on its own. It opens a menu: what is installed, install or update to the newest release, install an older one from the list, or remove Tuni with or without its settings. It installs the package built for the distribution it is run on, the RPM on Fedora, the deb on Debian and Ubuntu, the pkg.tar.zst on Arch.

A project can opt out of starting a new tab where the visible shell is, which is the exception the global setting has no way to express: one project opens its tabs where a fresh terminal would while the rest go on following the shell.

Fixed: a translucent window repaints whole, so a sliver of text no longer survives on chrome that has nothing opaque under it, and a glyph whose ink reaches past its cell is clipped to the grid instead of landing on the tab bar.

The scrollback is the depth the setting names. Upstream spends max_scrollback as bytes, so ten thousand lines used to buy about nine hundred rows and everything older was gone; the conversion now happens where every caller goes through, and a hit nine and a half thousand rows back is found.

An SFTP transfer says how far along it is, how fast it is going, and can be cancelled. A cancelled upload sweeps the truncated file at the far end, a cancelled download sweeps the local part file, and the press empties the queue behind it.

The Info page opens the project in an installed code editor, wearing the icon and name of the one picked last; the arrow lists the rest. Which editors exist is a PATH scan, so every install method is found.
A pane falls back to xterm-256color where xterm-ghostty has no terminfo, instead of buying "unknown terminal type" from every ncurses program.

The window chrome: the Git page wears a commit graph, New Project sits under the last project and stays sticky, dialogs go solid under a translucent window, and the pane grip lights only under the pointer rather than aliasing over whatever sits beneath it.

The window goes quiet when nobody is looking. The panel and diff polls skip their tick while it is inactive and catch up when activity returns, the scrollbar fade redraws only when its alpha moved, and the live search re-runs on the frame clock. The Info page's editor icons are looked up when the page first opens rather than before the first frame, which was 43 of the 49 milliseconds the panel cost at startup.
Fixed: a closed pane lets go of its handlers, its place in the tab recency list, its replay text and its textures, and a git child whose stdin write failed is reaped and reports what git itself said.

Clicks, drags and the wheel behave the way Ghostty's do. A press reaches the application the moment it happens, Shift takes the mouse back unless the application asked to keep it, a third click with Ctrl selects one command's output, a right click selects the word under the pointer, and the wheel spends its pixels a whole row at a time. A URL that is only text opens with Ctrl+click.
A copy is confirmed with a toast, including the copy an application makes over OSC 52, so a program that takes or clears the clipboard is seen doing it.
The editor drives a language server and a debugger with breakpoints, and a selection grows by syntax with Alt+Up. The settings choose the panel's pages and the window's shortcuts.
The window blur asks X11 as well as Wayland, and only a compositor that can blur is asked. Faint text draws halfway to the background.
Fixed: Escape closes the command palette, and a taken forward port names the process that actually holds the address.

The packages are compiled for the baseline processor rather than for the machine that built them. Until now a build made on a host with AVX-512 carried instructions that older and smaller processors do not have, and tuni stopped with an illegal instruction before its window appeared. Anyone who saw that crash wants this build.
A file dragged onto a terminal pane now lands on the prompt as a quoted argument, ready for whatever command is being typed, instead of being refused.
A project dragged in the sidebar is carried as the row itself, held at the point it was picked up, rather than as the toolkit's picture of a document.
Tuni speaks SSH. Hosts come from the ssh configuration it already reads and from a hosts file of its own, a new tab can be a host list, and panes on the same host share one connection.
A connection carries a file browser. Step into directories at the far end, drag files across in either direction, and make, rename or delete them there.
Forwarded ports are listed beside the connection and open or close while it is up.

Also: snippets typed into a pane by name, the keys in ~/.ssh listed with the commands that change them, a menu on a right click in the terminal, and a pane that runs something other than a login shell.
The terminal gained mouse reporting, focus reporting, and box drawing characters it strokes itself instead of asking the font.
The window gained background opacity, blur, and padding, an about dialog, and a settings window that carries more of the settings.
The Files panel stands beside the tab strip at full height and takes a typed path or a step to the parent directory the way a prompt would.
Fixed: panes that closed without being forgotten, a command palette that kept the window alive, and a resize that stranded the prompt.
First release.
